*The C3RB3R ransom note directs victims to a unique portal TOR-based URL, j3qxmk6g5sk3zw62i2yhjnwmhm55rfz47fdyfkhaithlpelfjdokdxad[.]onion* (https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/c3rb3r-ransomware-ongoing-exploitation-of-cve-2023-22518-targets-unpatched-confluence-servers/).
*Authentication Bypass vulnerability was a critical factor* (https://www.vicarius.io/vsociety/posts/authentication-bypass-in-confluence-cve-2023-22518).
*Atlassian CISO Bala Sathiamurthy stressed immediate action* (https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2023-22518-critical-atlassian-confluence-data-center-and-server-improper-authorization).
*Publicly accessible instances are at highest risk* (https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2023-22518-critical-atlassian-confluence-data-center-and-server-improper-authorization).
*Second critical flaw in a month* (https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2023-22518-critical-atlassian-confluence-data-center-and-server-improper-authorization).

title: StopRansomware LockBit 3.0 Ransomware Affiliates Exploit CVE 2023-4966 Citrix Bleed Vulnerability
content:
#### Description
CISA, FBI, MS-ISAC, and Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) are releasing this CSA to disseminate IOCs, TTPs, and detection methods associated with LockBit 3.0 ransomware exploiting CVE-2023-4966, labeled Citrix Bleed, affecting Citrix NetScaler web application delivery control (ADC) and NetScaler Gateway appliances.

This CSA provides TTPs and IOCs obtained from FBI, ACSC, and voluntarily shared by Boeing. Boeing observed LockBit 3.0 affiliates exploiting CVE-2023-4966, to obtain initial access to Boeing Distribution Inc., its parts and distribution business that maintains a separate environment. Other trusted third parties have observed similar activity impacting their organization.

Historically, LockBit 3.0 affiliates have conducted attacks against organizations of varying sizes across multiple critical infrastructure sectors, including education, energy, financial services, food and agriculture, government and emergency services, healthcare, manufacturing, and transportation. Observed TTPs for LockBit ransomware attacks can vary significantly in observed TTPs.

Citrix Bleed, known to be leveraged by LockBit 3.0 affiliates, allows threat actors to bypass password requirements and multifactor authentication (MFA), leading to successful session hijacking of legitimate user sessions on Citrix NetScaler web application delivery control (ADC) and Gateway appliances. Through the takeover of legitimate user sessions, malicious actors acquire elevated permissions to harvest credentials, move laterally, and access data and resources.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-325a
2. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar23-325a

#### Publication Date
November 21, 2023

#### Author(s)
CISA

enhanced.Incident: LockBit 3.0 Ransomware Affiliates Exploit CVE-2023-4966 Citrix Bleed Vulnerability
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident is the exploitation of CVE-2023-4966, a vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances. This vulnerability allows threat actors to bypass password requirements and multifactor authentication (MFA), leading to session hijacking and subsequent unauthorized access to systems. *Sensitive information disclosure and differential firmware analysis were key to understanding the vulnerability* (https://www.mandiant.com/resources/blog/session-hijacking-citrix-cve-2023-4966). **Publicly available exploits were used by attackers** (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-exploits-citrix-bleed-in-attacks-10k-servers-exposed/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: LockBit 3.0 ransomware affiliates.
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The attack targeted Boeing Distribution Inc., a subsidiary of Boeing, and other organizations across various critical infrastructure sectors including education, energy, financial services, food and agriculture, government and emergency services, healthcare, manufacturing, and transportation. *The Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) was also a target* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-exploits-citrix-bleed-in-attacks-10k-servers-exposed/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The exploitation activity was identified as early as August 2023. The advisory was released on November 21, 2023. *Zero-day exploitation of the vulnerability was also observed by Mandiant starting in late August 2023* (https://www.mandiant.com/resources/blog/session-hijacking-citrix-cve-2023-4966). *Citrix advisory updated on October 17, 2023, and CISA added CVE-2023-4966 to their KEV catalog* (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/10/25/etr-cve-2023-4966-exploitation-of-citrix-netscaler-information-disclosure-vulnerability/).
enhanced.Impact: The specific number of records leaked or financial losses is not mentioned, but the impact includes unauthorized access to critical infrastructure sectors and potential data breaches. *Approximately 10,000 servers were exposed to this vulnerability* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-exploits-citrix-bleed-in-attacks-10k-servers-exposed/).
Mitigation: Isolate NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances for testing until patching is ready and deployable.
Upgrade vulnerable NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances to the latest version available to lower the risk of compromise.
Implement application controls to manage and control the execution of software, including allowlisting remote access programs.
Strictly limit the use of RDP and other remote desktop services.
Restrict the use of PowerShell and enable enhanced PowerShell logging.
Configure the Windows Registry to require User Account Control (UAC) approval for any PsExec operations.
Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers.
Require all accounts with password logins to comply with NIST's standards for developing and managing password policies.
Keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date. Prioritize patching known exploited vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems.

*Citrix recommended killing all active sessions using specific commands* (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/10/25/etr-cve-2023-4966-exploitation-of-citrix-netscaler-information-disclosure-vulnerability/).

Detection Signature.Signature name: Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway CVE-2023-4966 Exploitation
Internal checks: Ensure that Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances are patched to the latest versions.
Monitor for suspicious login patterns and unexpected changes in user session activities.
Analyze memory core dump files for signs of exploitation.
External scanning: Scan for vulnerable Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances.
Check for publicly accessible NetScaler ADC and Gateway instances.

IoCs: Domains: adobe-us-updatefiles[.]digital, assist.zoho.eu, eu1-dms.zoho[.]eu, fixme[.]it, unattended.techinline[.]net

Tools: TeamViewer, AnyDesk, Splashtop, Atera, Action1, ScreenConnect, Zoho Assist, *AssetNote released a proof-of-concept exploit demonstrating how session tokens can be stolen* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/lockbit-ransomware-exploits-citrix-bleed-in-attacks-10k-servers-exposed/), *XScan tool observed* (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/threat-brief-cve-2023-4966-netscaler-citrix-bleed/#:~:text=Details%20of%20the%20Vulnerability,10%2C%202023.).

title: Exploring FBot   Python-Based Malware Targeting Cloud and Payment Services
content:
#### Description
FBot is a Python-based hacking tool distinct from other cloud malware families, targeting web servers, cloud services, and SaaS platforms like AWS, Office365, PayPal, Sendgrid, and Twilio. Key features include credential harvesting for spamming attacks, AWS account hijacking tools, and functions to enable attacks against PayPal and various SaaS accounts. 

FBot has several features that target payment services as well as SaaS configurations. The PayPal Validator feature validates PayPal account status by contacting a hardcoded URL with an email address read from an input list. The email is added to the request in the customer details section to validate whether an email address is associated with a PayPal account. 

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/exploring-fbot-python-based-malware-targeting-cloud-and-payment-services/

#### Publication Date
January 11, 2024

#### Author(s)
Alex Delamotte

enhanced.Incident: Shanghai Police Datalake Leak
enhanced.Root cause: Misconfigured cloud services allowing unauthorized access. Specifically, FBot targets AWS, Office365, PayPal, Sendgrid, Twilio, and *content management systems (CMS)* (https://thehackernews.com/2024/01/new-python-based-fbot-hacking-toolkit.html), exploiting weak or default credentials, lack of multi-factor authentication (MFA), and unsecured API keys. *FBot checks AWS SES configurations and EC2 service quotas* (https://duo.com/decipher/fbot-hacking-tool-targets-cloud-payment-platforms).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Likely linked to iDevXploit, a handle associated with the development and deployment of FBot malware.
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Cloud and SaaS platforms such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Office365, PayPal, Sendgrid, and Twilio.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: July 2022 – January 2024 (as indicated by the sample timeline in the analysis).
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
T1003.005: Credential Dumping: Cloud Instance Metadata API
enhanced.Impact: The FBot malware is designed to steal credentials for cloud services, leading to potential hijacking of accounts, spamming attacks, and unauthorized access to sensitive data. *FBot can validate PayPal-associated email addresses, generate SendGrid API keys, and check Twilio account information* (https://duo.com/decipher/fbot-hacking-tool-targets-cloud-payment-platforms). *It uses an Indonesian technology service provider to validate email addresses* (https://redskyalliance.org/xindustry/exploring-fbot).
Mitigation: Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all cloud services and SaaS accounts.
Regularly review and rotate API keys and access credentials.
Monitor for new user accounts and significant configuration changes.
Secure web server configurations and ensure all endpoints are protected with strong, unique passwords.
Regularly update and patch software to mitigate vulnerabilities.
Employ intrusion detection systems (IDS) to monitor for suspicious activity related to credential harvesting or unauthorized access.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: Enable MFA on all accounts with programmatic access.
Create alerts for new user account creation and for significant changes in configuration.
Regularly scan for open ports and unsecured services.
Use strong, unique passwords and rotate them regularly.
Review and restrict permissions for API keys and access tokens.
Employ endpoint protection and monitoring tools to detect and respond to suspicious activity.

Detection Signature.Port: Various (depending on the service; typically HTTP/HTTPS ports 80/443 for APIs)
Internal checks: Setting1: Ensure AWS IAM policies are configured with the principle of least privilege.
Setting2: Ensure no default or weak passwords are in use.
Setting3: Ensure API keys are not hardcoded in configuration files and are rotated regularly.
External scanning: Open ports corresponding to exposed APIs.
Unusual login attempts or access patterns.

IoCs: Password: MCDonald2021D#1337 (hardcoded AWS IAM User password)
Additional Information: *Reverse IP scanners* (https://thehackernews.com/2024/01/new-python-based-fbot-hacking-toolkit.html) are used to generate random IP addresses and validate PayPal accounts via a *Lithuanian fashion designer's retail sales website* (https://thehackernews.com/2024/01/new-python-based-fbot-hacking-toolkit.html). FBot also includes features to check for *AWS Simple Email Service (SES)* email configuration details and EC2 service quotas (https://thehackernews.com/2024/01/new-python-based-fbot-hacking-toolkit.html).

*SentinelLabs* (https://securityboulevard.com/2024/01/python-fbot-hacking-cloud-and-saas-platforms-targeted/) identified that FBot does not use the Androxgh0st credential scraping module, distinguishing it with connections to the *Legion cloud information stealer* (https://securityboulevard.com/2024/01/python-fbot-hacking-cloud-and-saas-platforms-targeted/). *New user accounts with administrative privileges* (https://securityboulevard.com/2024/01/python-fbot-hacking-cloud-and-saas-platforms-targeted/) were created during infiltrations. Alex Delamotte from SentinelLabs emphasized the importance of basic security hygiene to prevent over-privileged credentials from being exploited (https://securityboulevard.com/2024/01/python-fbot-hacking-cloud-and-saas-platforms-targeted/).
FBot is unique for its functions targeting SaaS and payment services, including AliensFox, Predator, Greenbot (https://redskyalliance.org/xindustry/exploring-fbot).

title: NSPX30 A Sophisticated AitM-Enabled Implant Evolving Since 2005
content:
#### Description
ESET researchers uncover NSPX30, a sophisticated implant used by a new China-aligned APT group they have named Blackwood. NSPX30 is a sophisticated implant delivered through adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) attacks hijacking update requests from legitimate software. 

The implant was detected in targeted attacks against Chinese and Japanese companies, as well as against individuals located in the United Kingdom. NSPX30 is a multistage implant that includes several components such as a dropper, an installer, loaders, an orchestrator, and a backdoor. Both of the latter two have their own sets of plugins. The implant was designed around the attackers’ capability to conduct packet interception, enabling NSPX30 operators to hide their infrastructure. NSPX30 is also capable of allowlisting itself in several Chinese antimalware solutions.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/nspx30-sophisticated-aitm-enabled-implant-evolving-since-2005/

#### Publication Date
January 24, 2024

#### Author(s)
Facundo Muñoz

enhanced.Incident: NSPX30: A sophisticated AitM-enabled implant evolving since 2005. *ESET researchers* (https://dailysecurityreview.com/cyber-security/blackwood-hackers-use-aitm-to-hijack-wps-office-update-and-install-nspx30-malware/). *The implant exploits Jenkins server vulnerabilities including CVE-2024-23897* (https://mandos.io/newsletter/brief-36-apt29-targets-hpe-microsoft-blackwood-apt-nspx30-menace-more/).
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause is the adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) attack that hijacks update requests from legitimate software such as Tencent QQ, WPS Office, and Sogou Pinyin. Attackers use packet interception to deliver the NSPX30 implant via software updates, hiding their command and control servers. *The NSPX30's modern variant evolved from Project Wood and does not rely on DNS spoofing, instead utilizing a network implant within routers* (https://www.packetlabs.net/posts/blackwood-apt-uses-aitm-attacks-to-target-software-updates/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Blackwood, a China-aligned APT group. *Blackwood possibly shares access with other Chinese APT groups, such as Evasive Panda, LuoYu, and LittleBear* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackwood-hackers-hijack-wps-office-update-to-install-malware/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Victims include Chinese and Japanese companies, individuals in China, Japan, and the UK, a high-profile UK public research university, a large Chinese manufacturing and trading company, and a Japanese corporation's engineering and manufacturing office in China.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The implant evolution traced back to 2005, with significant activity since 2018. *Blackwood APT has been active since at least 2018* (https://www.packetlabs.net/posts/blackwood-apt-uses-aitm-attacks-to-target-software-updates/). A surge of malicious activity was detected in 2020. *NSPX30 evolved from DCM (Dark Specter), first seen in 2008* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackwood-hackers-hijack-wps-office-update-to-install-malware/).
MITRE TTPs: T1059.001: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1059.003: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
T1059.005: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
T1548.002: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Bypass User Account Control
T1562.001: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
T1036.005: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
T1027.009: Obfuscated Files or Information: Embedded Payloads
T1218.011: System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
T1560.002: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Library
T1074.001: Data Staged: Local Data Staging
T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
T1048.003: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
enhanced.Impact: Multiple organizations and individuals in China, Japan, and the UK were targeted, with data such as credentials, chat logs, contact lists, and audio conversations being exfiltrated. *NSPX30 can allowlist itself within several Chinese anti-malware solutions* (https://www.packetlabs.net/posts/blackwood-apt-uses-aitm-attacks-to-target-software-updates/). The exact number of records or financial losses is not specified.
Mitigation: 1. Secure software update mechanisms by enforcing HTTPS and ensuring integrity checks.
2. Implement network segmentation to limit the spread of malicious traffic.
3. Regularly update and patch network appliances to mitigate vulnerabilities.
4. Deploy advanced threat detection solutions that can identify and block adversary-in-the-middle attacks.
5. Educate employees about the risks of software updates and the importance of verifying sources.
6. Implement robust endpoint protection with behavior-based detection capabilities.
7. Ensure proper network monitoring to detect anomalies in traffic patterns.

Internal checks: Ensure all software update requests use HTTPS.
Monitor network traffic for unencrypted HTTP requests to software update domains.
Check for anomalies in DNS traffic related to legitimate software update servers.
Detection Signature.External scanning: Scan for open HTTP ports (port 80) on external network interfaces.

title: Kimsuky Group Uses AutoIt to Create Malware (RftRAT, Amadey)
content:
#### Description
The Kimsuky threat group, deemed to be supported by North Korea, has been active since 2013. At first, they attacked North Korea-related research institutes in South Korea before attacking a South Korean energy corporation in 2014. Cases of attacks against countries other than South Korea have also been identified since 2017. The group usually employs spear phishing attacks against the national defense sector, defense industries, the press, the diplomatic sector, national organizations, and academic fields to steal internal information and technology from organizations.

Even until recently, the Kimsuky group was still mainly employing spear phishing attacks to gain initial access. What makes the recent attacks different from the previous cases is that more LNK shortcut-type malware are being used instead of malware in Hangul Word Processor (HWP) or MS Office document format. The threat actor led users to download a compressed file through attachments or download links within spear phishing emails. When this compressed file is decompressed, it yields a legitimate document file along with a malicious LNK file.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/59590/

#### Publication Date
December 7, 2023

#### Author(s)
Sanseo

enhanced.Incident: Kimsuky Group Uses AutoIt to Create Malware (RftRAT, Amadey)
enhanced.Root cause: The primary root cause behind the incident is the successful execution of spear phishing attacks that led to the download and execution of malicious LNK files. These files contained scripts that installed remote control malware such as XRat, Amadey, and RftRAT. The vulnerabilities leveraged included weak user awareness and the lack of robust email filtering and endpoint protection.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Kimsuky Group (North Korea-supported threat actor, also known as Velvet Chollima, Thallium, BabyShark, KimJongRAT) *The changes* (https://apt.etda.or.th/cgi-bin/showcard.cgi?g=Kimsuky%2C%20Velvet%20Chollima)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Various sectors including national defense, defense industries, press, diplomatic sector, national organizations, and academic fields, primarily in South Korea.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The attacks mentioned in the report were ongoing throughout 2023.
MITRE TTPs: T1059.003: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
T1059.005: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
T1547.001: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
T1070.004: Indicator Removal on Host: File Deletion
enhanced.Impact: The impact is not quantified in terms of the number of records leaked or financial losses. However, the compromise involved unauthorized access to internal systems, leading to potential exfiltration of sensitive information, including internal documents, credentials, and other proprietary data.

Mitigation.User Awareness and Training: Educate users about the risks of spear phishing and the importance of verifying the authenticity of email senders and attachments.
Mitigation.Email Filtering: Implement advanced email filtering solutions to detect and block malicious attachments and links.
Mitigation.Endpoint Protection: Use robust endpoint protection solutions to detect and mitigate script-based malware.
Mitigation.Patch Management: Ensure that all systems and software are up-to-date with the latest security patches.
Mitigation.Network Segmentation: Segment the network to limit the spread of malware and restrict unauthorized access.
Mitigation.Regular Backups: Maintain regular backups of critical data and ensure they are stored securely and tested for integrity.

Detection Signature.Service: Windows Command Shell, Visual Basic Script

Internal checks.Setting1: Monitor for LNK file executions tied to script-based malware.
Internal checks.Setting2: Track abnormal processes spawned from LNK files (e.g., cmd.exe, wscript.exe).
Internal checks.Setting3: Detect persistence mechanisms such as registry run keys or startup folder entries.

enhanced.No IoCs found: Additional IoCs are available on AhnLab TIP.
enhanced.Conclusion: By following these mitigation steps and detection signatures, organizations can better protect themselves against similar spear phishing attacks and malware infections.

title: Trigona Ransomware Threat Actor Uses Mimic Ransomware
content:
#### Description
AhnLab Security Intelligence Center (ASEC) has identified a new activity of the Trigona ransomware threat actor installing Mimic ransomware.

The attack targets MS-SQL servers and exploits the Bulk Copy Program (BCP) utility in MS-SQL servers during the malware installation process. The attacker also attempted to use malware for port forwarding to establish an RDP connection to the infected system and control it remotely. The Trigona threat actor is known to use Mimikatz to steal account credentials. The threat actor installed AnyDesk to control the infected system.  Administrators must use passwords that cannot be easily guessed and change them periodically to protect the database servers from brute force and dictionary attacks. V3 must also be updated to the latest version to block malware infection in advance. Administrators should also use security programs such as firewalls for database servers accessible from outside to restrict access by external threat actors.

title: The Nine Lives of Commando Cat Analysing a Novel Malware Campaign Targeting Docker
content:
#### Description
Cado researchers have discovered a new malware campaign called "Commando Cat" that targets exposed Docker API endpoints. The campaign is a cryptojacking campaign that leverages Docker as an initial access vector and mounts the host's filesystem before running a series of interdependent payloads directly on the host. The payloads are delivered to exposed Docker API instances over the internet.

The attacker instructs Docker to pull down a Docker image called cmd.cat/chattr. The cmd.cat project "generates Docker images on-demand with all the commands you need and simply point them by name in the docker run command." It is likely used by the attacker to seem like a benign tool and not arouse suspicion.

The attacker then creates the container with a custom command to execute. The primary purpose of the user.sh payload is to create a backdoor in the system by adding an SSH key to the root account, as well as adding a user with an attacker-known password. The tshd.sh script is responsible for deploying TinyShell (tsh), an open-source Unix backdoor written in C. The gsc.sh script is responsible for deploying a backdoor called gs-netcat, a souped-up version of netcat that can punch through NAT and firewalls. The aws.sh script is a credential grabber that pulls credentials from a number of files on disk, as well as IMDS, and environment variables. The final payload is delivered as a base64 encoded script rather than in the traditional curl-into-bash method used previously by the malware. This base64 is echoed into base64 -d, and then piped into bash.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.cadosecurity.com/the-nine-lives-of-commando-cat-analysing-a-novel-malware-campaign-targeting-docker/

#### Publication Date
February 1, 2024

#### Author(s)
Nate Bill  
Matt Muir

enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Targeting Docker environments, which are commonly used across various industries and cloud service providers (AWS, GCP, Azure).

enhanced.Impact: The campaign resulted in cryptojacking, credential theft, and backdoor installation on Docker hosts. Financial losses include increased operational costs due to unauthorized compute resource usage and potential data breaches.
Mitigation: Secure Docker API Endpoints: Ensure Docker API endpoints are not exposed to the internet. Use firewall rules or security groups to restrict access. Use authentication and TLS to secure Docker API endpoints.
Regular Security Audits and Monitoring: Regularly audit Docker configurations and running containers. Implement continuous monitoring solutions to detect unusual activity.
Apply Principle of Least Privilege: Ensure that Docker containers and services run with the minimum necessary privileges. Avoid using root user within containers.
Implement Network Segmentation: Isolate Docker hosts and containers in dedicated network segments. Implement strict network policies to control inbound and outbound traffic.
Update and Patch Systems: Ensure Docker and underlying operating systems are up-to-date with the latest security patches.
Use Cloud Security Features: Leverage cloud provider security features like AWS IMDSv2 to protect instance metadata.

Setting2: Docker API should be secured with TLS and authentication.

title: Ransomware Spotlight Magniber
content:
#### Description
Formerly known as a successor of Cerber, the Magniber ransomware was primarily distributed via the Magnitude exploit kit and exclusively targeted South Korea in 2017. In 2018, it expanded its targets across Asia using CVE-2018-8174 for initial access.  In October 2022, phishing attacks were reported to distribute the Magniber ransomware using standalone JavaScript files digitally signed with a malformed key, exploiting the zero-day vulnerability CVE-2022-44698 to bypass Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) security warnings, and allowing malicious files to be executed without raising alerts. Microsoft later patched this vulnerability in December 2022.

Magniber was also previously known to use typosquatting, a technique that involves using domains similar to legitimate websites to lure users into downloading a ransomware payload. Trend Micro also observed Magniber distributing itself through fake installers with APPX and MSI formats in the first quarter of 2022.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/security/news/ransomware-spotlight/ransomware-spotlight-magniber

#### Publication Date
January 26, 2023

#### Author(s)
Trend Micro

enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident includes multiple vulnerabilities exploited by the Magniber ransomware. These include: CVE-2022-44698: Zero-day vulnerability to bypass Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) security warnings; CVE-2021-26411, CVE-2021-40444, and CVE-2021-34527 (PrintNightmare): Exploited for initial access; Other vulnerabilities like CVE-2016-0189, CVE-2018-8174, CVE-2019-1367, CVE-2020-0968, and *CVE-2023-24880* (https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/resource/blog/cve-2023-24880-vulnerability-exploited-by-magniber-ransomware-group).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Magniber ransomware operators (likely part of a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) model) *financially motivated threat actors* (https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/magniber-ransomware-actors-used-a-variant-of-microsoft-smartscreen-bypass/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The blog mentions multiple industries being targeted, including education, government, manufacturing, healthcare, and technology. Initially, it mainly targeted Asian countries, but has since expanded globally, affecting countries such as Taiwan, South Korea, Australia, Turkey, and Japan *with over 100,000 downloads since January 2023* (https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/magniber-ransomware-actors-used-a-variant-of-microsoft-smartscreen-bypass/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The attack has been ongoing since its initial detection in 2017, resurfaced in 2021, and continues to operate as of the latest data from 2022.

Mitigation.1. Audit and Inventory: Take inventory of all assets and data; Identify authorized and unauthorized devices and software; Audit event and incident logs regularly.
Mitigation.2. Configure and Monitor: Manage hardware and software configurations; Grant administrative privileges only when necessary; Monitor network ports, protocols, and services; Activate security configurations on network infrastructure devices; Establish a software allowlist.
Mitigation.3. Patch and Update: Conduct regular vulnerability assessments; Perform patching or virtual patching for operating systems and applications; Update software and applications to their latest versions.
Mitigation.4. Protect and Recover: Implement data protection, backup, and recovery measures; Enable multifactor authentication (MFA).
Mitigation.5. Secure and Defend: Employ sandbox analysis to block malicious emails; Deploy the latest versions of security solutions across all layers of the system; Use advanced detection technologies such as those powered by AI and machine learning.
Mitigation.6. Train and Test: Regularly train and assess employees on security skills; Conduct red-team exercises and penetration tests.

title: Following the Scent of TrickGate 6-Year-Old Packer Used to Deploy the Most Wanted Malware
content:
#### Description
Initially observed in July 2016, TrickGate is a shellcode-based packer offered as a service to hide malware from EDRs and antivirus programs, also referred to as “Crypter” and “FUD” on hacking forums.  TrickGate has been involved in wrapping some of the best-known top-distribution malware families, such as Cerber, Trickbot, Maze, Emotet, REvil, CoinMiner, Cobalt Strike, DarkVNC, BuerLoader, HawkEye, NetWire, AZORult, Formbook, Remcos, Lokibot, AgentTesla, and many more.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://research.checkpoint.com/2023/following-the-scent-of-trickgate-6-year-old-packer-used-to-deploy-the-most-wanted-malware/

#### Publication Date
January 30, 2023

#### Author(s)
Arie Olshtein

enhanced.Incident: TrickGate Packer
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident is the utilization of a shellcode-based packer called TrickGate, which has been used to deploy various malware by hiding it from Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and antivirus programs. Vulnerable services include email servers and web browsers that are prone to phishing attacks involving malicious links and attachments. *The initial infection vector includes a Zoom job interview email* (https://www.gosecure.net/blog/2021/12/03/trickbot-leverages-zoom-work-from-home-interview-malspam-heavens-gate-and-spamhaus/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Various threat actors, including Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups, have used TrickGate to deploy multiple types of malware such as Cerber, Trickbot, Maze, Emotet, REvil, Cobalt Strike, AZORult, Formbook, AgentTesla, and more. *The attack often starts with a malicious NSIS installer* (https://medium.com/@baglai.vlad/formbook-malware-uses-trickgate-loader-946cc3dcff40).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The primary targets are organizations in the manufacturing sector, but TrickGate also affects education, healthcare, finance, and business enterprises. The attacks are globally distributed, with a focus on regions such as Taiwan and Turkey.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Initially observed in July 2016 and continues to be active.

title: Roaming Mantis Implements New DNS Changer In Its Malicious Mobile App
content:
#### Description
Roaming Mantis (a.k.a Shaoye) is a long-term cyberattack campaign that uses malicious Android package (APK) files to control infected Android devices and steal data. In 2022, Kaspersky observed a DNS changer function implemented in its Android malware Wroba.o.

Back in 2018, Kaspersky first saw Roaming Mantis activities targeting the Asian region, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. At that time, the criminals compromised Wi-Fi routers for use in DNS hijacking, which is a very effective technique. It was identified as a serious issue in both Japan and South Korea. Through rogue DNS servers, all users accessing a compromised router were redirected to a malicious landing page. From mid-2019 until 2022, the criminals mainly used smishing instead of DNS hijacking to deliver a malicious URL as their landing page. The landing page identified the user’s device platform to provide malicious APK files for Android or redirect to phishing pages for iOS.  Users with infected Android devices that connect to free or public Wi-Fi networks may spread the malware to other devices on the network if the Wi-Fi network they are connected to is vulnerable.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://securelist.com/roaming-mantis-dns-changer-in-malicious-mobile-app/108464/


#### Publication Date
January 19, 2023

#### Author(s)
GReAT

enhanced.Incident: Roaming Mantis DNS Changer in Malicious Mobile App
enhanced.Root cause: The Roaming Mantis group exploits vulnerable Wi-Fi routers via a DNS changer function in their malicious Android malware, Wroba.o/Agent.eq, to hijack DNS settings on Wi-Fi routers. This enables redirection of traffic to malicious landing pages and installation of *Trojanized applications facebook.apk and chrome.apk* (https://securelist.com/roaming-mantis-uses-dns-hijacking-to-infect-android-smartphones/85178/). They also deploy the *XLoader payload* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/roaming-mantis-hits-android-and-ios-users-in-malware-phishing-attacks/) on Android devices and use base64 encoded Imgur profile destinations to retrieve C2 configurations. The campaign employs *smishing tactics* (https://www.phishprotection.com/cybersecurity/infamous-smishing-campaign-roaming-mantis-hits-users-france) to trick users into clicking malicious URLs. The malware uses *kuronekoyamato.apk* (https://securelist.com/roaming-mantis-reaches-europe/105596/) to deliver its payload.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Roaming Mantis (a.k.a Shaoye)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Targets include users in South Korea, Japan, France, Germany, the United States, Taiwan, Turkey, and other regions. *French users* (https://www.phishprotection.com/cybersecurity/infamous-smishing-campaign-roaming-mantis-hits-users-france) are currently being specifically targeted.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Ongoing since at least 2018 with significant activity in 2022.
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
enhanced.Impact: Numerous infected devices and compromised Wi-Fi routers in targeted regions. Specific download statistics include 24,645 APK downloads in Japan, 7,354 in Austria, and 7,246 in France. The malware's malicious payload, *test.dex* (https://securelist.com/roaming-mantis-uses-dns-hijacking-to-infect-android-smartphones/85178/), significantly impacts users. The campaign also involves *phishing page for Apple credentials* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/roaming-mantis-hits-android-and-ios-users-in-malware-phishing-attacks/). Additionally, *SEKOIA cybersecurity firm* (https://www.phishprotection.com/cybersecurity/infamous-smishing-campaign-roaming-mantis-hits-users-france) reports significant activity targeting *French users*. The malware now includes *backdoor commands* (https://securelist.com/roaming-mantis-reaches-europe/105596/) to steal photos and galleries from infected devices.
Mitigation: Change default credentials on Wi-Fi routers to strong, unique passwords.
Regularly update router firmware to patch known vulnerabilities.
Use security solutions capable of detecting and mitigating threats like HEUR:Trojan-Dropper.AndroidOS.Wroba.o or HEUR:Trojan-Dropper.AndroidOS.Agent.eq.
Implement network segmentation to isolate critical systems from insecure devices.
Educate users on the risks of connecting to public Wi-Fi networks and encourage the use of VPNs.

Internal checks: Ensure default admin credentials are changed.
Verify firmware is up-to-date.
Monitor DNS settings for unauthorized changes.
External scanning: Detect open admin interfaces on default ports.
Check for known vulnerable router models.

enhanced.Detection of suspicious activities: *Permissions to receive/read/write/send SMS/MMS and record audio* (https://securelist.com/roaming-mantis-uses-dns-hijacking-to-infect-android-smartphones/85178/) and attempts to steal *verification codes for two-factor authentication* (https://securelist.com/roaming-mantis-uses-dns-hijacking-to-infect-android-smartphones/85178/) can signal potential compromise. The campaign uses *obfuscation techniques* (https://securelist.com/roaming-mantis-reaches-europe/105596/) to evade detection.

title: Threat Actors Exploit Progress Telerik Vulnerability in U.S. Government IIS Server
content:
#### Description
From November 2022 through early January 2023, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and authoring organizations identified the presence of indicators of compromise (IOCs) at a federal civilian executive branch (FCEB) agency. Analysts determined that multiple cyber threat actors, including an APT actor, were able to exploit a .NET deserialization vulnerability (CVE-2019-18935) in Progress Telerik user interface (UI) for ASP.NET AJAX, located in the agency’s Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) web server. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability allows for remote code execution. According to Progress Software, Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX builds before R1 2020 (2020.1.114) are vulnerable to this exploit.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-074a

#### Publication Date
March 13, 2023

#### Author(s)
CISA

enhanced.Incident: Exploitation of Progress Telerik Vulnerabilities in U.S. Government IIS Servers
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause is the exploitation of a .NET deserialization vulnerability (CVE-2019-18935) in Progress Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX's RadAsyncUpload function, leading to remote code execution on Microsoft IIS servers. Additionally, exploitation of CVE-2017-9248 in the Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX DialogHandler component and the presence of CVE-2017-11317 were identified. Exploiting JavaScriptSerializer Deserialization in RadAsyncUpload can execute malicious code in the context of the w3wp.exe process. Markus Wulftange of Code White GmbH and Paul Taylor (@bao7uo) assisted in making this information public *The changes* (https://docs.telerik.com/devtools/aspnet-ajax/knowledge-base/common-allows-javascriptserializer-deserialization). CVE-2019-18935 has a severity score of 9.8 and affects versions from 2011.1.315 to 2019.3.1023; the vulnerability is listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog as CWE-502: deserialization of untrusted data *The changes* (https://www.twingate.com/blog/tips/cve-2019-18935#:~:text=CVE%2D2019%2D18935%20is%20a,315%20to%202019.3.).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Multiple threat actors, including an advanced persistent threat (APT) actor and the cybercriminal actor XE Group.
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Targeted entities were multiple U.S. Government IIS Servers.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: From November 2022 to early January 2023, with additional activity identified as late as April 2023.

T1505.003: Server Software Component: Web Shell
T1036.005: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location

Mitigation: Implement a centralized log collection and monitoring capability.

Upgrade all instances of Telerik UI ASP.NET AJAX to the latest version, preferably R1 2020 or later *The changes* (https://docs.telerik.com/devtools/aspnet-ajax/knowledge-base/common-allows-javascriptserializer-deserialization).

title: Bad Magic New APT Found in the Area of Russo-Ukrainian Conflict
content:
#### Description
Since the start of the Russo-Ukrainian conflict, Kaspersky researchers and the international community at large have identified a significant number of cyberattacks executed in a political and geopolitical context. In October 2022, Kaspersky identified an active infection of government, agriculture and transportation organizations located in the Donetsk, Lugansk, and Crimea regions. 

Although the initial vector of compromise is unclear, the details of the next stage imply the use of spear phishing or similar methods. The victims navigated to a URL pointing to a ZIP archive hosted on a malicious web server.  When the potential victim activates the LNK file included in the ZIP file, it triggers a chain of events that lead to the infection of the computer with a previously unseen malicious framework that we named CommonMagic. The malware and techniques used in this campaign are not particularly sophisticated, but are effective, and the code has no direct relation to any known campaigns.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://securelist.com/bad-magic-apt/109087/

#### Publication Date
March 21, 2023

#### Author(s)
Leonid Bezvershenko  
Igor Kuznetsov  
Georgy Kucherin

enhanced.Incident: Bad Magic: New APT Found in the Area of Russo-Ukrainian Conflict
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause includes: - Use of malicious LNK files with double extensions (e.g., .pdf.lnk) leading to malware infection upon opening. - The infection chain involves downloading a malicious MSI file that acts as a dropper package, containing an encrypted payload and a decoy document. - The dropper uses a VBS script to execute an embedded PowerShell script that decrypts the next stage malware. - The backdoor, named PowerMagic, leverages cloud storage services like OneDrive and Dropbox for command and control (C&C) communication. *Additionally, the CloudWizard framework builds on CommonMagic with modules for keylogging, microphone recording, USB data stealing, and more* (https://www.normcyber.com/bulletins/norm-threat-bulletin-31st-may-2023/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The specific threat actor behind the Bad Magic campaign is not yet attributed to any known group. The campaign is still active, and ongoing investigations may reveal more details *including the potential involvement of a new threat group* (https://www.broadcom.com/support/security-center/protection-bulletin/new-threat-group-leveraging-powermagic-backdoor-and-commonmagic-framework). *Characteristics of CloudWizard match previous APT campaigns in Ukraine, such as Operation Groundbait and Operation BugDrop* (https://www.normcyber.com/bulletins/norm-threat-bulletin-31st-may-2023/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The victims targeted by this campaign include government, agriculture, and transportation organizations located in the Donetsk, Lugansk, and Crimea regions. *Kaspersky researchers* (https://social.cyware.com/news/new-apt-found-actively-using-powermagic-backdoor-and-commonmagic-framework-b49856b5) identified an active infection. *New victims have also been found in diplomatic and research organizations in central and western Ukraine* (https://www.normcyber.com/bulletins/norm-threat-bulletin-31st-may-2023/). *Additionally, administrative organizations were targeted* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/commonmagic-targets-russo/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The campaign was identified in October 2022 *by Kaspersky researchers* (https://social.cyware.com/news/new-apt-found-actively-using-powermagic-backdoor-and-commonmagic-framework-b49856b5). The blog was published on March 21, 2023, indicating ongoing activity. *The group has been active since at least September 2021* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/commonmagic-targets-russo/).

enhanced.Impact: The exact number of records leaked or devices affected is not specified. The impact includes unauthorized access to sensitive information and potential disruption of services.
enhanced.Mitigation: 1. **User Awareness Training:** Educate users about the risks of opening unsolicited email attachments and clicking on suspicious links. 2. **Email Filtering:** Implement advanced email filtering to detect and block malicious attachments and links. 3. **Endpoint Protection:** Use endpoint protection solutions with capabilities to detect and block malicious scripts and executables. 4. **Cloud Storage Security:** Monitor and restrict the use of cloud storage services for unauthorized data exfiltration. 5. **Regular Patching:** Ensure that all systems and software are regularly updated with the latest security patches. 6. **Network Segmentation:** Implement network segmentation to limit the spread of malware within the organization. 7. **Incident Response Plan:** Develop and regularly update an incident response plan to quickly address and mitigate security incidents.

title: Word Documents Disguised as Normal MS Office URLs Being Distributed - ASEC BLOG
content:
#### Description
AhnLab Security Emergency response Center (ASEC) reported on a case of malware disguised as a Word document being distributed through through various ways, such as KakaoTalk group chats. The ASEC analysis team discovered that the URL used in the fake Word document is disguised to closely resemble the normal URL. Some of the malicious document filenames included names of individuals that are specialists in the field of diplomatic security. The filenames were also related to North Korea, China, surveys, or diplomatic security.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/42554/


#### Publication Date
November 24, 2022

#### Author(s)
jcleebobgatenet

enhanced.Incident: Word Documents Disguised as Normal MS Office URLs Being Distributed
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause is the use of Template Injection in Word documents, where malicious URLs are cleverly disguised to resemble legitimate MS Office URLs, exploiting user trust and similar URL appearances to deceive users. *Template Injection in settings.xml.rels is used* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/jp/42683/). This technique evades security tools by using a popular *Highly Evasive Adaptive Threat (HEAT)* technique, and Legacy URL Reputation Evasion (LURE), wherein attackers use websites categorized as having a good reputation by web filters to deliver malware * (https://www.menlosecurity.com/blog/isolation-a-vaccine-for-template-injection-attacks). Additionally, attackers can employ *HTML smuggling* and *Clickjacking in HTML* to further bypass security measures * (https://www.senturean.com/posts/21_03_16_ways_of_phishing_01/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The blog does not specify the exact threat actor but mentions the malware as 'Downloader/DOC.Kimsuky,' suggesting the involvement of the Kimsuky group, known for targeting South Korean entities. The document also mentions the use of *Empire and Phishery frameworks to create weaponized template injection documents* (https://www.menlosecurity.com/blog/isolation-a-vaccine-for-template-injection-attacks).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The targets include specialists in diplomatic security, with filenames related to North Korea, China, surveys, or diplomatic security, suggesting victims in the diplomatic and security sectors, particularly in South Korea. *The malicious documents are being distributed through KaKaoTalk group chats* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/42233/). Additionally, *hijacking existing email thread conversations* is another infection vector used by adversaries to distribute these weaponized documents * (https://www.menlosecurity.com/blog/isolation-a-vaccine-for-template-injection-attacks).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The attack was ongoing around November 2022, as indicated by the publication date of the blog post (Nov 17, 2022).
MITRE TTPs: T1203 - Exploitation for Client Execution: Exploiting vulnerabilities in Word documents.
T1071.001 - Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols: Using URLs to download and execute malicious templates.
T1193 - Spearphishing Attachment: Distributing malicious documents through phishing.
enhanced.Impact: The precise impact in terms of the number of devices or financial losses is not mentioned. However, given the nature of the targets (diplomatic security specialists), the impact could involve significant breaches of sensitive information. The technique is noteworthy for evading security tools and solutions using *Living off the Land (LotL)* attacks, where legitimate software is used to perform malicious actions * (https://www.menlosecurity.com/blog/isolation-a-vaccine-for-template-injection-attacks). The use of *macro-enabled DOTM templates* and *registry key modification* techniques further enhances the attack's stealth * (https://www.senturean.com/posts/21_03_16_ways_of_phishing_01/).
Mitigation: Update antivirus software (e.g., V3) to the latest version to detect and block the malicious documents.
Avoid opening document files from unknown sources.
Confirm the legitimacy of files even if they are forwarded from credible users.
Implement email filtering and attachment scanning to detect and block malicious attachments.
Educate users on recognizing phishing attempts and suspicious URLs.

Detection Signature.Incident: Word Documents Disguised as Normal MS Office URLs
Detection Signature.Signature name: Malicious Template Injection in Word Documents
Internal checks: Monitor for external URL references in Word document templates.
Verify the authenticity of URLs in Word document templates.
Use endpoint protection to detect and block known malicious document signatures.
External scanning: Scan incoming emails and attachments for known indicators of compromise (IoCs).
Use URL filtering to block access to known malicious domains referenced in the attack.

*(월드코리안) 시진핑 제3기 출범의 함의와 향후 전망.docx* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/42233/)

title: Warning for Office Outlook Privilege Escalation Vulnerability (CVE-2023-23397)
content:
#### Description
Microsoft has discovered a vulnerability in Outlook for Windows that is being exploited to steal NTLM credentials.

Learn more about CVE-2023-23397 here: [CVE-2023-23397 Microsoft Outlook elevation of privilege vulnerability leads to NTLM credential theft](/articles/1bccfe3f)

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/50218/
2. [CVE-2023-23397 Microsoft Outlook elevation of privilege vulnerability leads to NTLM credential theft](/articles/1bccfe3f)

#### Publication Date
March 22, 2023

#### Author(s)
gygy0101
references: [CVE-2023-23397 Microsoft Outlook elevation of privilege vulnerability leads to NTLM credential theft](/articles/1bccfe3f)

Incident: Microsoft Office Outlook Privi.Root cause: Vulnerable Microsoft Outlook 'Reminder' feature allowing exploitation via the PidLidReminderFileParameter and PidLidReminderOverride properties.
Incident: Microsoft Office Outlook Privi.Threat Actor/group/campaign: *Microsoft Threat Intelligence* (https://msrc.microsoft.com/blog/2023/03/microsoft-mitigates-outlook-elevation-of-privilege-vulnerability) discovered limited, targeted abuse linked to a *Russia-based threat actor* (https://msrc.microsoft.com/blog/2023/03/microsoft-mitigates-outlook-elevation-of-privilege-vulnerability), specifically attributed to *APT28 (Fancy Bear/Strontium)* (https://socprime.com/blog/microsoft-outlook-vulnerability-cve-2023-23397-detection/#:~:text=CVE%2D2023%2D23397%20is%20a%20vulnerability%20that%20specifically%20targets%20Microsoft,the%20PidLidReminderFileParameter%20extended%20MAPI%20property.), also known as *Forest Blizzard (STRONTIUM)* (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/03/24/guidance-for-investigating-attacks-using-cve-2023-23397/).
Incident: Microsoft Office Outlook Privi.Organization/industry/location: Microsoft Outlook users, particularly in government, transportation, energy, and military sectors in Europe.
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol - Web Protocols
T1552.001: Unsecured Credentials - Credentials In Files
Incident: Microsoft Office Outlook Privi.Impact: Potential theft of NTLM credentials from users who receive malicious emails exploiting this vulnerability, leading to Net-NTLMv2 hashes exposure and *relay attacks* (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/threat-brief-cve-2023-23397). The vulnerability, with a *CVSS base score of 9.8* (https://socprime.com/blog/microsoft-outlook-vulnerability-cve-2023-23397-detection/#:~:text=CVE%2D2023%2D23397%20is%20a%20vulnerability%20that%20specifically%20targets%20Microsoft,the%20PidLidReminderFileParameter%20extended%20MAPI%20property.), is triggered by an attacker sending a message with a *UNC path to SMB share* on an untrusted network, allowing NTLM negotiation message theft. It is a *zero-touch exploit* requiring no user interaction (https://socprime.com/blog/microsoft-outlook-vulnerability-cve-2023-23397-detection/#:~:text=CVE%2D2023%2D23397%20is%20a%20vulnerability%20that%20specifically%20targets%20Microsoft,the%20PidLidReminderFileParameter%20extended%20MAPI%20property.).
Mitigation: Add users to the Protected Users Security Group to prevent NTLM from being used as an authentication mechanism. Note: This may affect applications that require NTLM.
Block outbound TCP 445/SMB from the network to prevent SMB relay attacks.
Apply the March 2023 security update for Outlook for Windows.

Use the *Exchange scanning script* (https://socprime.com/blog/microsoft-outlook-vulnerability-cve-2023-23397-detection/#:~:text=CVE%2D2023%2D23397%20is%20a%20vulnerability%20that%20specifically%20targets%20Microsoft,the%20PidLidReminderFileParameter%20extended%20MAPI%20property.) and the CVE-2023-23397.ps1 script to detect and clean up any exploitation attempts in Exchange environments.

Internal checks: Check for the presence of emails with malicious PidLidReminderFileParameter and PidLidReminderOverride properties.
Ensure NTLM is disabled in Protected Users Security Group.
Verify outbound TCP 445/SMB is blocked.
Detection Signature.External scanning: Use provided PowerShell script (CVE-2023-23397.ps1) to scan Exchange environments.

Incident: Microsoft Office Outlook Privi.*Additional entities*: The US government conducted a *disruption operation* against Forest Blizzard infrastructure in *January 2024* (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/03/24/guidance-for-investigating-attacks-using-cve-2023-23397/). The Polish Cyber Command (DKWOC) partnered with Microsoft to mitigate techniques used by this actor.

title: Deobfuscating the Recent Emotet Epoch 4 Macro
content:
#### Description
Recently, Trustwave SpiderLabs saw Emotet switch focus to using OneNote attachments, which is a tactic also adopted by other malware groups in recent months. This analysis is intended to help the cybersecurity community better understand the wider obfuscation and padding tricks Emotet is using.  

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.trustwave.com/en-us/resources/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/deobfuscating-the-recent-emotet-epoch-4-macro/

#### Publication Date
April 3, 2023

#### Author(s)
Rodel Mendrez  
Joshua Deacon

enhanced.Incident: Emotet Epoch 4 Macro Campaign
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind this incident is the use of highly obfuscated VBA macros in combination with a new tactic of compressing bloated document files into ZIP files. This campaign from Emotet involves the use of OneNote attachments to deliver the malicious payload, leveraging zero-byte padding techniques to inflate file sizes and evade security scanners *and bypass Microsoft macro block* (https://blog.checkpoint.com/security/march-2023s-most-wanted-malware-new-emotet-campaign-bypasses-microsoft-blocks-to-distribute-malicious-onenote-files/).

enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Not specified (General targets of Emotet campaigns include various industries and geographical locations)
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Early March 2023 – Ongoing
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol - Web Protocols
T1059.005: Command and Scripting Interpreter - Visual Basic
enhanced.Impact: The impact of this campaign includes the potential compromise of infected systems, leading to data theft, further malware distribution, and potential financial losses depending on the scope of the infection. Attackers gather user email data such as login credentials and contact information, expanding the campaign's reach *using malicious OneNote files and fake message trick* (https://blog.checkpoint.com/security/march-2023s-most-wanted-malware-new-emotet-campaign-bypasses-microsoft-blocks-to-distribute-malicious-onenote-files/). *Additionally, attackers have utilized Qakbot, Bumblebee Loader, and Redline Stealer, with WSF files embedded in OneNote documents for payload delivery* (https://www.esentire.com/blog/pulse-check-on-onenote-for-malware-delivery).
Mitigation: Update email security gateways to detect and block malicious attachments, especially those using zero-byte padding techniques.
Implement advanced threat detection tools capable of analyzing and deobfuscating VBA macros.
Educate employees on recognizing phishing attempts and suspicious attachments.
Regularly update antivirus and endpoint protection software to detect and block Emotet-related payloads.
Employ network segmentation to limit the spread of the malware if an infection occurs.

Internal checks.Setting1: Block emails with attachments exceeding typical size limits for document files.
Internal checks.Setting2: Analyze email attachments for zero-byte padding techniques.
Internal checks.Setting3: Use sandboxing to open and analyze email attachments before delivery.

External scanning.Monitor for outbound connections to know: Detect and block suspicious download attempts from email attachments.

Additional Modules.*Outlook Scraper*: *Scrapes names and email addresses from victims’ Outlook accounts* (https://www.logpoint.com/en/blog/emotet-ually-unstable-the-resurgence-of-a-nuisance/)
Additional Modules.*MailPass View*: *Reveals passwords and account details from email clients* (https://www.logpoint.com/en/blog/emotet-ually-unstable-the-resurgence-of-a-nuisance/)
Additional Modules.*WebBrowserPassView*: *Recovers passwords from browsers like Chrome, Firefox* (https://www.logpoint.com/en/blog/emotet-ually-unstable-the-resurgence-of-a-nuisance/)

title: MERCURY and DEV-1084 Destructive attack on hybrid environment
content:
#### Description
Microsoft Threat Intelligence has detected destructive operations enabled by MERCURY, a nation-state actor linked to the Iranian government, that attacked both on-premises and cloud environments. While the threat actors attempted to masquerade the activity as a standard ransomware campaign, the unrecoverable actions show destruction and disruption were the ultimate goals of the operation.

Previous MERCURY attacks have been observed targeting on-premises environments, however, the impact in this case notably also included destruction of cloud resources. Microsoft assesses that MERCURY likely worked in partnership with another actor that Microsoft tracks as DEV-1084, who carried out the destructive actions after MERCURY’s successful operations had gained access to the target environment.

MERCURY likely exploited known vulnerabilities in unpatched applications for initial access before handing off access to DEV-1084 to perform extensive reconnaissance and discovery, establish persistence, and move laterally throughout the network, oftentimes waiting weeks and sometimes months before progressing to the next stage. DEV-1084 was then later observed leveraging highly privileged compromised credentials to perform en masse destruction of resources, including server farms, virtual machines, storage accounts, and virtual networks, and send emails to internal and external recipients.

In this blog post, we detail our analysis of the observed actor activity and related tools. We also share information to the community and industry partners on ways to detect these attacks, including detection details of MERCURY and DEV-1084’s tools in Microsoft 365 Defender, Microsoft Defender for Identity, Microsoft Defender for Cloud Applications, Microsoft Defender Antivirus, and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. As with any observed nation-state actor activity, Microsoft has directly notified targeted or compromised customers, providing them with important information needed to secure their environments.

Microsoft uses DEV-#### designations as a temporary name given to an unknown, emerging, or a developing cluster of threat activity, allowing Microsoft to track it as a unique set of information until we reach high confidence about the origin or identity of the actor behind the activity.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/04/07/mercury-and-dev-1084-destructive-attack-on-hybrid-environment/

#### Publication Date
April 7, 2023

#### Author(s)
Microsoft Security Threat Intelligence

enhanced.Incident: MERCURY and DEV-1084: Destructive attack on hybrid environment
enhanced.Root cause: Exploitation of unpatched vulnerabilities (e.g., Log4j 2) in internet-facing devices, followed by lateral movement and privilege escalation using compromised credentials.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: MERCURY (linked to Iranian government, also known as MuddyWater, Boggy Serpens, Earth Vetala, and Cobalt Ulster) and DEV-1084 (now tracked as Mango Sandstorm and Storm-1084, respectively), presenting as DarkBit for obfuscation. *MuddyWater* (https://cyware.com/news/new-dev-1084-group-linked-with-muddywater-carries-out-destructive-attacks-8a8bda38).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Not explicitly mentioned in the document.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Attack observed in April 2023.
MITRE TTPs: Initial Access: Exploitation of Public-Facing Application (T1190)
Credential Access: Credentials from Password Stores (T1555)
Lateral Movement: Remote Services (T1021), Remote Service Session Hijacking (T1563)
Command and Control: Application Layer Protocol (T1071.001)
enhanced.Impact: Destruction of cloud resources including server farms, virtual machines, storage accounts, and virtual networks. Email impersonation and potential data exfiltration. *Access via Exchange Web Services* (https://cyware.com/news/new-dev-1084-group-linked-with-muddywater-carries-out-destructive-attacks-8a8bda38).
Mitigation: Secure on-prem environment with strong credential hygiene and tamper protection.
Enable Conditional Access policies and continuous access evaluation in Azure AD.
Regularly apply security patches and updates to all systems.
Implement least privilege access and multifactor authentication (MFA) for all accounts.
Monitor and audit logs for suspicious activity and implement advanced threat detection solutions like Microsoft 365 Defender and Microsoft Sentinel.

Secure On-Prem Environment: Enable tamper protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
Regularly review and update security policies and Group Policy Objects (GPOs).
Deploy and maintain security patches for all hardware and software.
Secure Azure AD Environment: Enable Conditional Access policies to enforce device compliance and trusted IP address requirements.
Enable continuous access evaluation to revoke access in real-time based on user condition changes.
Regularly monitor Azure AD logs for unusual activities, such as unfamiliar sign-in properties.
Implement Advanced Threat Detection: Use Microsoft 365 Defender and Microsoft Sentinel for real-time threat detection and response.
Configure alerts and detection rules for signs of compromise, such as unusual resource deletions or privilege escalation activities.

Detection Signature.Incident: Unauthorized Access and Destruction of Cloud Resources
Internal checks: Ensure Conditional Access policies are enabled.
Monitor activity logs for unusual sign-ins and actions by privileged accounts.
Review and restrict permissions of service accounts regularly.
External scanning: Monitor for external IP addresses associated with known threat actors.
Detect unauthorized OAuth applications and administrative consent actions.

title: Magecart Threat Actor Rolls Out Convincing Modal Forms
content:
#### Description
While following up on an ongoing Magecart credit card skimmer campaign, Malwarebytes discovered threat actors using original logos from compromised stores and customized web elements known as a modal to hijack the checkout page. While the technique to insert frames or layers is not new, the remarkable thing is that the skimmer looks more authentic than the original payment page.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intelligence/2023/04/kritec-art

#### Publication Date
April 27, 2023

#### Author(s)
Jérôme Segura

enhanced.Incident: Magecart threat actor rolls out convincing modal forms
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident is the injection of a malicious JavaScript skimmer into websites using the PrestaShop CMS. The skimmer uses a fraudulent modal designed to steal credit card information by mimicking the legitimate payment process of the compromised sites. *The skimmer code is heavily obfuscated with base64* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-swap-stealth-for-realistic-checkout-forms-to-steal-credit-cards/). *The skimmer also impersonates legitimate third-party vendors like Google Tag Manager as an evasion technique* (https://thehackernews.com/2023/04/attention-online-shoppers-dont-be.html).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Magecart (including the specific campaign using the Kritec skimmer first detected in March 2022)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The affected industries are e-commerce stores, including a Parisian travel accessory store, e-commerce sites in Denmark and Finland, and several other e-commerce sites in different languages (e.g., Dutch and Finnish stores) *The changes* (https://blog.koddos.net/hackers-hijack-online-stores-to-display-fake-payment-forms-and-steal-credit-cards/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Not explicitly mentioned, but the article indicates the campaign was ongoing and has been tracked in recent months (as of April 2023).
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
enhanced.Impact: Multiple e-commerce sites compromised, with unknown specific numbers of records or financial losses. *The skimmer drops a cookie on users to prevent loading the malicious modal again on the same or another site* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-swap-stealth-for-realistic-checkout-forms-to-steal-credit-cards/). *Jerome Segura, director of threat intelligence at Malwarebytes, noted the skimmer looks more authentic than the original payment page* (https://thehackernews.com/2023/04/attention-online-shoppers-dont-be.html).
Mitigation: Regularly audit and monitor your web applications and third-party scripts loaded on your website.
Implement Content Security Policy (CSP) to restrict the sources from which scripts can be loaded.
Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) to ensure that fetched resources (scripts, styles) are delivered without unexpected manipulation.
Employ a web application firewall (WAF) to detect and block common threats.
Regularly update and patch CMS and plugins to prevent exploitation of known vulnerabilities.
Educate employees about the importance of validating third-party integrations and the potential risks of skimmers.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: Conduct regular security reviews and audits of your website, including all third-party components.
Implement CSP headers to restrict script sources:
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' https://trusted.cdn.com;
Use SRI for external resources:
<script src='https://trusted.cdn.com/script.js' integrity='sha384-oqVuAfXRKap7fdgcCY5uykM6+R9GqQ8K/ux7+S/9cC5Q6+3P3pLsF6B6cQ+Yl/2z' crossorigin='anonymous'></script>
Deploy and configure a WAF to filter and monitor HTTP traffic to and from your web application.
Regularly update the CMS, plugins, and all software components to the latest versions.
Train employees on recognizing and mitigating web skimmer threats.

Internal checks: Setting1: Regularly audit JavaScript files loaded on the checkout page.
Setting2: Regularly monitor the integrity of the payment process flow.
Setting3: Implement and monitor CSP and SRI to detect unauthorized script loads.
External scanning: Detect unauthorized JavaScript files being loaded (e.g., [name of store]-loader.js).

title: Chain Reaction ROKRAT’s Missing Link
content:
#### Description
Check Point Research (CPR) continues to track the evolution of ROKRAT and its delivery methods.

In previous years, ROKRAT infection chains usually involved a malicious Hangul Word Processor (HWP, a popular document format in South Korea) document with an exploit, or a Microsoft Word document with macros. While some ROKRAT samples still use these techniques, Checkpoint have observed a shift to delivering ROKRAT with LNK files disguised as legitimate documents. This shift is not exclusive to ROKRAT but represents a larger trend that became very popular in 2022.

The lures used as part of the ROKRAT infections are largely focused on South Korean foreign and domestic affairs. Most of those lures are in Korean, suggesting the targets are Korean-speaking individuals.

Checkpoint's findings suggest that various multi-stage infection chains used to eventually load ROKRAT were utilized in other attacks, leading to the deployment of additional tools affiliated with the same actor. Those tools include another custom backdoor, GOLDBACKDOOR, and the commodity malware Amadey.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://research.checkpoint.com/2023/chain-reaction-rokrats-missing-link/

#### Publication Date
May 1, 2023

#### Author(s)
Check Point Research

These LNK files are often disguised as legitimate documents and execute PowerShell scripts to initiate multi-stage infection chains, ultimately leading to the deployment of the ROKRAT malware.

title: Kimsuky Evolves Reconnaissance Capabilities in New Global Campaign
content:
#### Description
Kimsuky is a North Korean advanced persistent threat (APT) group with a long history of targeted attacks across the world. Current understanding of the group indicates they are primarily assigned to intelligence collection and espionage operations in support of the North Korean government since at least 2012.  In 2018 the group was observed deploying a malware family dubbed BabyShark, and SentinelOne's latest observations indicate the group has evolved the malware with an expanded reconnaissance capability – SentinelOne refers to this BabyShark component as ReconShark.

Historically, Kimsuky targets have been located across countries in North America, Asia, and Europe. In the groups latest campaigns, they continue their global targeting themed around various ongoing geopolitical topics. For example, the latest Kimsuky campaigns have focused on nuclear agendas between China and North Korea, relevant to the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine.

title: New Phishing-As-A-Service Tool “Greatness” Already Seen In The Wild
content:
#### Description
A previously unreported phishing-as-a-service (PaaS) offering named “Greatness” has been used in several phishing campaigns since at least mid-2022. Greatness incorporates features seen in some of the most advanced PaaS offerings, such as multi-factor authentication (MFA) bypass, IP filtering and integration with Telegram bots.

Greatness, for now, is only focused on Microsoft 365 phishing pages, providing its affiliates with an attachment and link builder that creates highly convincing decoy and login pages. It contains features such as having the victim’s email address pre-filled and displaying their appropriate company logo and background image, extracted from the target organization’s real Microsoft 365 login page. 

An analysis of the domains targeted in several ongoing and past campaigns revealed the victims were almost exclusively companies in the U.S., U.K., Australia, South Africa, and Canada, and the most commonly targeted sectors were manufacturing, health care and technology. 

To use Greatness, affiliates must deploy and configure a provided phishing kit with an API key that allows even unskilled threat actors to easily take advantage of the service’s more advanced features. The phishing kit and API work as a proxy to the Microsoft 365 authentication system, performing a “man-in-the-middle” attack and stealing the victim’s authentication credentials or cookies.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-phishing-as-a-service-tool-greatness-already-seen-in-the-wild/

#### Publication Date
May 10, 2023

#### Author(s)
Tiago Pereira

enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Unknown affiliates using the Greatness PaaS.
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Targeted sectors include manufacturing, health care, technology, and real estate. Geographic focus includes the U.S., U.K., Australia, South Africa, and Canada. Greatness mainly targets businesses using Microsoft 365, especially in the U.S. and U.K. *The changes* (https://medium.com/hunter-strategy/cti-notification-greatness-phishing-kit-9ccecf0e0667)

T1556.001: Modify Authentication Process: Multi-factor Authentication Interception
enhanced.Impact: Compromise of Microsoft 365 accounts, theft of authentication credentials, and session cookies. The exact financial losses or number of affected individuals are not specified.
Mitigation: Educate employees about phishing attacks and how to recognize suspicious emails.
Implement and enforce robust email filtering to detect and block phishing emails.
Enable MFA for all accounts, preferably using methods less susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks, such as hardware tokens.
Regularly review and update incident response plans to address phishing attacks.

Use anti-phishing tools and services to detect and block phishing attempts in real-time.

The Vade Threat Intelligence and Response Center (TIRC) and *Talos’s GitHub repository IoCs/2023/04* have provided crucial indicators of compromise. Further, the campaign is linked to *United Bangladeshi Hackers (UBH TEAM)*, which has been active with webshells and phishing campaigns. *Greatness incorporates advanced features like IP filtering, Telegram bots integration, pre-filling victim’s email, and displaying the target's company logo* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/greatness-phishing-exploits/). The campaign also employs *Business Email Compromise (BEC)* tactics and sends phishing emails with an *HTML attachment* that, when opened, leads to a fake Microsoft 365 login page *configured via a user-facing control panel* within the phishing kit. *Cisco Talos researchers identified three components* of Greatness: the phishing kit, an API, and a Telegram bot or email address *The changes* (https://medium.com/hunter-strategy/cti-notification-greatness-phishing-kit-9ccecf0e0667).

title: Newly Identified RA Group Compromises Companies in U.S. and South Korea With leaked Babuk Source Code
content:
#### Description
Talos recently discovered a new ransomware actor, RA Group, who emerged in April 2023 and seems to be using leaked Babuk source code in its attacks. After an alleged member of the Babuk group leaked the full source code of its ransomware in September 2021, various ransomware families have emerged leveraging the leaked Babuk code. 

The group is launching double extortion attacks. Like other ransomware actors, RA Group also operates a data leak site in which they threaten to publish the data exfiltrated from victims who fail to contact them within a specified time or do not meet their ransom demands. This form of double extortion increases the chances that a victim will pay the requested ransom.

RA Group deploys their ransomware with a built-in ransom note specifically written to each victim with their name on it, a common practice among ransomware groups. However, it is unusual that RA Group names the victim in the executable, as well.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ra-group-ransomware/


#### Publication Date
May 15, 2023

#### Author(s)
Chetan Raghuprasad

enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident is the use of the leaked Babuk ransomware source code by the RA Group. The RA Group has customized the Babuk ransomware to target specific victims, including providing unique ransom notes and executing specific encryption and deletion commands. *Custom encryption algorithms are employed* (https://www.hivepro.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/RA-Groups-Custom-Ransomware-Hits-US-South-Korea_TA2023230.pdf).
